title: After striking out on the top free agent (again), the Blue Jays turn to Japan
summary: CBC Sports' daily newsletter breaks down the Toronto Blue Jays' signing of Japanese star Kaima Taira after they were turned down by the No. 1 player on the market.

image.caption: Newly acquired Blue Jays pitcher Kaima Taira played for Japan at the Tokyo Olympics and became a star in his country's version of the major leagues. (Kazuhiro Fujihara/AFP via Getty Images)

blocks.text: MLB·THE BUZZER
CBC Sports' daily newsletter breaks down the Toronto Blue Jays' signing of Japanese star Kaima Taira after they were turned down by the No. 1 player on the market.
Toronto moves on from Skubal by signing Seibu Lions star
The Buzzer Newsletter | This is a segment from CBC's weekday sports newsletter. | Sign up here to receive full versions of The Buzzer directly in your inbox.
For four straight years now, the Toronto Blue Jays have been "in on" the top player in free agency, only to come up short.

During the Shohei Ohtani mania of December 2023, online sleuths scoured everything from private jet flight paths to sushi restaurant reservations for clues before the modern-day Babe Ruth (predictably) turned down Toronto for a bigger offer from the Los Angeles Dodgers. In 2024, star outfielder Juan Soto chose the New York Mets, and last year Kyle Tucker joined Ohtani on the Dodgers.

The clear No. 1 free agent this off-season was Tarik Skubal, a 30-year-old left-handed starter who won back-to-back Cy Young Awards with Detroit before the non-contending Tigers sent him to the Dodgers at the trade-deadline in August. The Blue Jays were among a handful of teams making a serious effort to land Skubal and reportedly offered him a nine-year contract worth more than $400 million US. But the Mets, who had the biggest payroll in baseball this year, nabbed him on Sunday for nine years and $450M — the largest deal ever for a pitcher in terms of both total money and average annual value. (Interestingly, the famously free-spending Dodgers reportedly never made a formal offer amid owner Mark Walter's ongoing legal troubles.)
The good news is that, after getting outbid so many times, the Jays seem to have become pretty adept at refocusing on the other fish in the sea.

Last year, perhaps sensing that they weren't going to land Tucker and that shortstop Bo Bichette was not going to return on favourable terms (sure enough, he too signed with the Mets), Toronto proactively poached strikeout artist Dylan Cease from San Diego with a seven-year, $210M US contract. It turned out to be a savvy move as Cease led the American League in strikeout rate and finished second in Cy Young voting, though he did wear down as the season went on and ended up on the injured list with a shoulder issue that did not require surgery. Later, the Jays dipped into Japan to sign Kazuma Okamoto as their new third baseman, and he went on to lead the team with 33 home runs (more than double anyone else's total) despite striking out a ton.
Today, the Jays sort of blended those two signings, reportedly agreeing to a five-year, $80M contract with Japanese import Kaima Taira. It's their first big move of the off-season.

Taira is a 27-year-old right-handed starting pitcher who stands just 5-foot-8. As ESPN's excellent baseball writer Jeff Passan notes here, Taira is two inches shorter than any starter in Major League Baseball this year. But he weighs a solid 218 pounds and averaged a powerful 95.7 miles per hour on his fastball this season for the Seibu Lions, making him the hardest-throwing starter in Japan's version of the major leagues. He hit 100 mph on the radar gun this year, and he's said to deploy eight different types of pitches.

Taira, who played for Japan at the 2021 Olympics in Tokyo, spent six of his first pro seasons as a reliever before converting back to a starter this year. The Nippon Professional Baseball website shows he posted a miniscule 1.36 ERA in 146 innings while allowing just 95 hits, striking out 141 batters and walking 45. He also surrendered only four home runs.

If his effectiveness translates to the majors, Taira could give Toronto a formidable top three starters alongside Cease and Trey Yesavage, the 2025 playoff sensation who was derailed by injuries this year. And it's possible that the Jays are not done yet.
Other pitching options dwindling

Jays GM Ross Atkins may have felt pressure to sign Taira after some other possible Plan B starting pitchers went off the market over the last 24 hours. Former Baltimore left-hander Trevor Rogers reportedly agreed to an unexpectedly large five-year, $120M contract with the Chicago Cubs last night and, earlier today, the Orioles replaced Rogers by luring righty Freddy Peralta from Tampa Bay with a reported five-year, $125M deal.

If the Jays want to make further upgrades to their rotation, they could look to the likes of Michael King, a crafty 32-year-old right-hander who had a 132 ERA+ (meaning he was 32 per cent better than the league average) for San Diego this year; Tyler Mahle, another 32-year-old righty who posted a 1.99 ERA after being traded to Atlanta at the August deadline; or even 35-year-old Kevin Gausman, who was Toronto's ace for a few years before they shipped him to the Cubs that same day as they slipped out of contention. If the Jays are looking to shore up their bullpen, the top guy on the market is flamethrowing lefty Adrian Morejon, who struck out 11.2 batters per nine innings this year with the Padres and is viewed by some as a potential starter.
What about the bats?

But we all know that pitching was not the reason the Jays went from being one play away from winning the World Series against the mighty Dodgers to finishing dead last in the AL East. Toronto ranked ninth in the majors in team ERA this year — up from 19th in 2025.

The main causes of Toronto's downfall, besides a slew of injuries to key players, came at the plate. While the Jays still hit for a pretty good average and were very difficult to strike out, they plummeted from No. 1 in the majors in on-base percentage in 2025 down to a three-way tie for 25th while experiencing a stunning power outage. Among the 30 big-league teams, Toronto finished last in home runs (they were 11th in 2025) and 26th in slugging percentage (down from seventh). As a result, they scored a major-league-low 648 runs — more than 200 fewer than the MLB-leading Cubs.

The poster boy for Toronto's anemic offence was Vladimir Guerrero Jr., who went from the toast of Canada with his eight homers in 18 post-season games in 2025 to mustering just nine in 144 games this year, including a grand total of one at home. Vladdy also posted the lowest batting average and slugging percentage of his eight-year career and his worst on-base percentage for a full season.

Seeing as how Guerrero was worth a pretty inconsequential 1.1 Wins Above Replacement this year, a generous person could argue that a return to form by the superstar slugger would basically amount to a big free-agent acquisition. A less-generous person might say that Guerrero better bounce back because he still has 13 years left on the titanic 14-year, $500M extension he signed in April 2025.

But that's all spilled milk under the bridge. If the Jays don't want to just bank on a quick rebound by Guerrero and the rest of the everyday lineup, they have some options to add a bat in free agency.

One potential spot to target is the corner outfield, where the options include Seiya Suzuki, who averaged 29 homers the last two years with the Cubs; and Randy Arozarena, a rookie sensation with Tampa a few years ago who had 26 homers and 26 stolen bases this season for Seattle. But a big piece came off the board today when Japanese league MVP Teruaki Sato agreed to a reported six-year, $120M deal with the Cubs as Chicago continued its spending spree.

There's also the middle infield. If the Jays aren't sold on Ernie Clement at second base (we all love him, but his .285 on-base percentage this year left a lot to be desired), they might consider the Yankees' Jazz Chisholm Jr. He racked up 31 homers and 31 steals in 2025 and, despite regressing at the plate this year, remained a valuable player with his high-quality baserunning and defence. Another candidate at second is Pittsburgh's Brandon Lowe, who improved his weak defensive play this year while reaching the 30-homer plateau for the second straight time. But he also strikes out a lot, which the Jays don't like.
Lockout looming

Whatever direction the Jays choose, they may have to act fast. The current collective bargaining agreement expires one week from tonight, at which point the owners will almost certainly lock out the players and all business will be suspended until a new CBA is hammered out.
That could take awhile. The owners are hell-bent on getting a salary cap for the first time in baseball history, while the players are very much against it.

At the moment, there's little urgency to make a deal as spring training is still 2½ months away and Opening Day is four months from today. Both sides know those are the real deadlines, so we're still in the sabre-rattling and exchanging-half-hearted-proposals stage.

But, judging by all the big signings that have gone down in the last few days, teams are clearly feeling the heat to make moves before the big shutdown. We'll see whether the Blue Jays stay in on the action.
